t: Find the Degree of Each Vertex
o: Given an undirected graph's adjacency matrix, the degree of vertex i is the number of 1s in row i (the matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, so rows and columns agree). Example 1's triangle gives [2,2,2]; Example 2 gives [1,1,0]; a single vertex gives [0]. With n <= 100, summing each row is all that is needed.
k: Degree of i = row sum of matrix[i]; symmetry makes column sums redundant.

a.i: Simply count 1s in each row of the adjacency matrix.
s: For each row i, sum matrix[i][j] over j.
Collect the sums into the answer array.
a.t: O(n^2) — every matrix entry inspected once.

a.i: Because the graph is undirected, summing column j gives the same degree; computing both and asserting equality is a nice sanity check, and column sums are what you would use for directed in-degrees.
s: For each column j, sum matrix[i][j] over i.
Return the column sums as the degree array.

w: Row sums are the natural answer; mention column sums only to exploit/check symmetry. Pitfall: if the matrix ever had self-loops (diagonal 1s), each would count twice in the degree — here the constraints forbid them. Edge cases: n = 1 (answer [0]). Follow-up: adjacency-list input (same row-sum idea, O(V+E)), or directed graphs where in/out degrees differ.
